notes: Flat blue-green needles 4-7 cm long that curve upward; native to western North America.
Glossy dark green flat needles with two white bands underneath and a notched tip; from the Caucasus, grown as a Christmas tree.
Small leaf with 3-5 rounded lobes and smooth edges; milky sap in the leaf stalk. European ornamental.
Small three-lobed leaf with a long middle lobe and double-toothed edges; turns bright red in fall. Asian ornamental that spreads into natural areas.
Compound leaf with 3 leaflets; known for peeling cinnamon-coloured bark. Chinese ornamental.
Compound leaf with 3-5 irregularly toothed leaflets; the only Ontario maple with compound leaves.
Small leaf deeply cut into 5-9 pointed lobes like an open hand. Japanese ornamental.
Large three-lobed leaf with fine double teeth, shaped like a goose foot; green-and-white striped bark. Understory tree of northern forests.
Broad five-lobed leaf with a few pointed teeth; milky sap oozes from a snapped leaf stalk (sugar maple's sap is clear).
Large thick five-lobed leaf with coarse round teeth and a pale underside. European tree.
Three-lobed leaf with toothed margins and V-shaped sinuses; pale underside and often a reddish leaf stalk.
Deeply cut five-lobed leaf with sharp teeth; silvery-white underside.
Five-lobed leaf with smooth U-shaped sinuses and few teeth; clear sap from a snapped leaf stalk.
Palmately compound leaf with 5 finely toothed leaflets on short stalks; native to the Appalachians.
Palmately compound leaf with 5 narrow leaflets; crushed leaves smell unpleasant. Native to the US Midwest; planted in Ontario.
Large palmately compound leaf with 5-7 broad, stalkless leaflets widest near the tip. European street tree.
Palmately compound leaf with 5 glossy leaflets; red tubular flowers. Native to the southeastern US.
Very long compound leaf with 11-25 leaflets, each with 1-2 glandular teeth near the base; crushed leaves smell rank.
Feathery twice-compound leaf with tiny leaflets; pink pom-pom flowers. Asian ornamental, rarely hardy in Ontario.
Oval leaf with fine teeth along most of the edge; young leaves are fuzzy underneath.
Oblong leaf with fine teeth; hairless when mature. Hard to tell from other serviceberries by the leaf alone.
Oval leaf with fine sharp teeth; young leaves are bronze-purple and hairless.
Large drooping leaf, widest past the middle, smooth edges; smells like green pepper when crushed. Carolinian zone tree.
Oval double-toothed leaf; twigs smell of wintergreen; shiny golden peeling bark. A major hardwood of Ontario's mixed forests.
Oval double-toothed leaf; bright white bark. Himalayan ornamental.
Oval leaf with fine sharp teeth; twigs smell strongly of wintergreen; dark cherry-like bark. Very rare in Ontario (Niagara region); a species at risk.
Diamond-shaped double-toothed leaf with a wedge-shaped base; shaggy salmon-coloured peeling bark. Native to the eastern US; planted in Ontario.
Triangular leaf with a long tapering tip and double teeth; flutters like a poplar leaf. Eastern Ontario.
Fuzzy, sandpapery leaf that can be unlobed or deeply lobed on the same tree. East Asian.
Oval double-toothed leaf with deeply impressed parallel veins. European ornamental.
Oval double-toothed leaf with straight parallel veins; smooth grey muscular-looking trunk.
Compound leaf with 7-11 slender leaflets; sulphur-yellow buds.
Compound leaf with usually 5 hairless leaflets. Uncommon in southern Ontario.
Compound leaf with usually 5 large leaflets, the top three biggest; bark peels in long shaggy strips.
Compound leaf with 7-9 leaflets, fuzzy underneath and fragrant when crushed. Rare in Ontario (Niagara region).
Long narrow leaf with sharp, hooked, bristle-tipped teeth. Endangered in Ontario after chestnut blight.
Large heart-shaped leaf in whorls of three, often with a short tip; smells unpleasant when crushed. Native to the southeastern US.
Large heart-shaped leaf in whorls of three with a longer tapering tip; almost identical to southern catalpa. Native to the central US; planted in Ontario.
Short blue-green needles in dense clusters on spur shoots. From North Africa.
Longer soft needles (up to 5 cm) in clusters on spur shoots; drooping branch tips. Himalayan.
Stiff dark green needles in clusters on spur shoots; flat-topped tiered branches.
Oval leaf with an uneven base, toothed edge and long tapering tip; warty bark.
Small hackberry leaf with few or no teeth. Rare in Ontario; a species at risk.
Small round heart-shaped leaf with rounded teeth; fallen leaves smell like burnt sugar. Japanese ornamental.
Smooth-edged heart-shaped leaf; pink flowers on bare branches in spring. Historically native on Pelee Island but considered gone from the wild; widely planted.
Flat sprays of scale-like leaves with white X-shaped marks underneath. Japanese ornamental.
Fine irregular sprays of small blue-green scales. Native to US Atlantic coast swamps.
Glossy oval leaf with smooth edges, opposite; white fringe-like flowers. East Asian.
Oval smooth-edged opposite leaf; fringe-like white flowers. Native to the southeastern US.
Compound leaf with 7-11 alternate leaflets; smooth grey bark. Native to the southeastern US.
Oval opposite leaf whose veins curve to follow the edge; white flower bracts. Endangered in Ontario (Carolinian zone).
Opposite oval leaf with wavy edges and curving veins; pointed white bracts. East Asian ornamental.
Small opposite oval leaf with curving veins; yellow flowers very early in spring. European.
Broad heart-shaped leaf with coarse double teeth. Street tree from southeastern Europe.
Glossy leaf widest near the tip, toothed only on the outer half; long sharp thorns.
Small leaf with 3-5 shallow rounded lobes; thorny. European ornamental.
Small triangular leaf with 3-5 sharp lobes, maple-like; slender thorns. Native to the southeastern US.
Oval toothed leaf with shallow lobes; fruit has a waxy bloom.
Glossy oval leaf with fine teeth and shallow lobes near the tip. Native to the southeastern US.
Awl-shaped needles that curve inward around the twig. Japanese.
Glossy oval leaf with smooth edges; blocky alligator-skin bark. Native to the southeastern US.
Glossy elm-like toothed leaf; torn leaves stretch thin latex threads. Chinese.
Opposite compound leaf with 7-11 glossy leaflets. East Asian ornamental.
Oval leaf with one straight vein ending in each tooth; smooth grey bark. Affected by beech bark disease and beech leaf disease.
Large rough leaf with 3-5 deep lobes. Mediterranean; not hardy outdoors in most of Ontario.
Opposite compound leaf with 5-9 leaflets; whitish underside. Devastated by the emerald ash borer.
Opposite compound leaf with 7-11 stalkless leaflets. Assessed as at risk in Ontario because of the emerald ash borer.
Opposite compound leaf with 5-9 leaflets, green on both sides. Devastated by the emerald ash borer.
Fan-shaped leaf with fine radiating veins, often notched in the middle. Chinese living fossil, common street tree.
Feathery compound or twice-compound leaf with small leaflets; wild trees have large branched thorns. Native to southwestern Ontario; thornless cultivars are common street trees.
Very large twice-compound leaf with oval leaflets. Threatened in Ontario.
Oval leaf with fine teeth and a pointed tip; white bell-shaped flowers. Native to the southeastern US.
Stiff evergreen leaf with spiny teeth. Native to the eastern US.
Compound leaf with 11-17 leaflets, a terminal leaflet usually present; sticky hairs. Endangered in Ontario due to butternut canker.
Compound leaf with 15-23 leaflets, the terminal one often missing. Southern Ontario.
Scale-like leaves on older shoots and sharp needles on young ones; blue berry-like cones.
Compound leaf with coarsely toothed, irregularly lobed leaflets; papery lantern-shaped pods. East Asian.
Soft needles in clusters on spur shoots, dropped in fall; larger cones than the native tamarack.
Star-shaped leaf with 5-7 pointed lobes; spiky ball fruit. Native to the southeastern US.
Distinctive four-lobed leaf with a flat, notched tip. Carolinian zone of southern Ontario.
Glossy oval leaf with a long tip; large green bumpy fruit; thorny. Native to the south-central US.
Large oval leaf with smooth edges and a pointed tip. Ontario's only native magnolia; endangered.
Oval leaf widest near the tip; white flowers before the leaves. Chinese ornamental.
Large thick glossy evergreen leaf, often rusty underneath. Native to the southeastern US; not hardy in Ontario.
Huge leaf (up to 80 cm) with an ear-shaped base. Native to the southeastern US.
Oval leaf widest near the tip; large pink-and-white flowers. Hybrid ornamental.
Small narrow leaf widest near the tip; star-shaped white flowers. Japanese ornamental.
Large leaf (to 50 cm) clustered at branch ends like an umbrella, tapering to the base. Native to the eastern US.
Narrow oval leaf with a silvery-white underside. Native to the US Atlantic coast.
Narrow oval leaf with shallow teeth. Native to the southeastern US.
Oval finely toothed leaf; small red or yellow fruit. Asian ornamental.
Oval leaf with coarse teeth and sometimes small lobes. Southern Ontario.
Small oval toothed leaf; pink buds opening white. Ornamental.
Oval finely toothed leaf with a long tip. Chinese ornamental.
Oval toothed leaf, fuzzy underneath. European/Asian; naturalized in Ontario from old orchards.
Soft flat needles in opposite pairs, shed in fall with the twig. Chinese living fossil.
Glossy leaf that can be unlobed or mitten-shaped; hybridizes with and threatens native red mulberry.
Rough sandpapery leaf, unlobed or lobed, with a long tip. Endangered in Ontario, partly from hybridizing with white mulberry.
Glossy oval leaf with smooth edges, brilliant red in fall. Uncommon in southern Ontario.
Oval double-toothed leaf like a birch; hop-like fruit clusters; shreddy bark.
Long narrow finely toothed leaf with a sour taste. Native to the southeastern US.
Huge fuzzy heart-shaped opposite leaf; purple flowers. East Asian; invasive in parts of the eastern US.
Opposite compound leaf with 5-13 leaflets; corky bark. East Asian; invasive in parts of the eastern US.
Square needles on drooping branchlets; very long cones (10-20 cm). European, widely planted and naturalized.
Very short (6-8 mm) blunt glossy needles. From the Caucasus.
Stiff sharp needles, often silvery blue. Native to the Rocky Mountains.
Stiff needles in bundles of 3; patchy camouflage bark. Chinese.
Needles in bundles of 5; dense narrow tree. Alps and Carpathians.
Slender needles in bundles of 2; orange-red upper bark. East Asian.
Flexible needles in bundles of 2 or 3. Native to the southeastern US.
Needles in bundles of 5; very flexible twigs. Native to the Rocky Mountains.
Needles in bundles of 5, edible pine nuts. East Asian.
Long stiff dark needles in bundles of 2. European, widely planted.
Short twisted needles in bundles of 5. Japanese ornamental.
Needles in bundles of 5. Balkans.
Stiff twisted needles in bundles of 2; very spiny cones. Appalachian.
Long needles in bundles of 2 that snap cleanly when bent; reddish plated bark.
Stiff needles in bundles of 3; tufts of needles can sprout from the trunk. Rare in Ontario (Thousand Islands area).
Soft flexible needles in bundles of 5. Ontario's provincial tree.
Twisted blue-green needles in bundles of 2; orange upper bark. European; naturalized and spreading in parts of southern Ontario.
Long needles in bundles of 3. Native to the southeastern US.
Stiff dark needles in bundles of 2; white buds. Japanese.
Short twisted needles in bundles of 2. Native to the eastern US.
Long drooping needles in bundles of 5. Himalayan.
Large maple-like leaf with 3-5 lobes; camouflage bark; fruit balls usually in pairs. Hybrid street tree.
Large maple-like leaf with shallow lobes; white patchy upper bark; single fruit balls. Southern Ontario river valleys.
Triangular leaf with coarse curved teeth and a flattened leaf stalk.
Round leaf with large coarse teeth and a flattened leaf stalk.
Round leaf with fine teeth and a flattened stalk that makes it flutter. Most widespread tree in North America.
Narrow shiny leaf with fine teeth and a long tip; shiny reddish bark with horizontal lenticels.
Oval sharply toothed leaf with a long tip, reddish when young. Japanese ornamental cherry.
Narrow glossy leaf with fine incurved teeth; often rusty hairs along the midrib underneath.
Oval leaf with bristle-tipped teeth and a long tip. Japanese ornamental.
Small narrow sharply toothed leaf; often a weeping form. Japanese ornamental.
Oval leaf with very fine sharp teeth, widest above the middle; dark astringent fruit in clusters.
Oval double-toothed leaf with a long tip. Japanese ornamental cherry (High Park, Toronto).
Soft flat needles in clusters on spur shoots, turning gold before falling. Chinese.
Compound leaf with 3 leaflets; papery round winged fruit. Lake Erie shoreline; a species at risk in Ontario.
Glossy oval leaf with wavy fine teeth. Chinese street tree; invasive in parts of the eastern US.
Long narrow chestnut-like leaf with bristle-tipped teeth. East Asian.
Leaf with 7-9 rounded lobes, no bristle tips.
Leaf widest near the tip with shallow rounded lobes or wavy teeth; whitish underside.
Narrow leaf with irregular pointed lobes; mossy acorn caps. European.
Deeply cut bristle-tipped lobes with C-shaped sinuses. Native to the eastern US.
Leaf with 3-5 bristle-tipped lobes, the end lobe long and curved. Native to the southeastern US.
Narrow leaf with smooth edges and a single bristle tip. Native to the US Midwest.
Leaf with a deep pair of sinuses near the middle and a broad wavy upper half; fringed acorn cap.
Leathery leaf shaped like a bell, broad at the tip with 3 shallow bristle-tipped lobes. Native to the southeastern US.
Leaf with large rounded teeth, widest near the tip. Native to the southeastern US.
Leaf with regular rounded teeth along the edge; thick ridged bark. Native to the eastern US.
Leaf with sharp, evenly spaced teeth (not lobes). Southern Ontario.
Small leaf widest at the tip, spoon-shaped with variable lobing. Native to the southeastern US.
Deeply cut bristle-tipped lobes with U-shaped sinuses; drooping lower branches. Southwestern Ontario; common street tree.
Narrow willow-like leaf with smooth edges and a bristle tip. Native to the southeastern US.
Rounded lobes with small ear-like lobes at the base of a very short leaf stalk. European; naturalized in places.
Leaf with 7-11 bristle-tipped lobes and moderately deep sinuses.
Deeply cut bristle-tipped lobes, glossy. Rare in southwestern Ontario; a species at risk.
Thick leaf with two large middle lobes giving a cross shape. Native to the southeastern US.
Glossy bristle-tipped lobed leaf; yellow-orange inner bark. Southern Ontario sandy sites.
Small thick evergreen leaf with smooth curled edges. Native to the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
Compound leaf with 7-19 small oval leaflets; paired thorns at the base of each leaf. Native to the southeastern US; spreads into open habitats in Ontario.
Long narrow finely toothed leaf on long hanging branches. Chinese.
Narrow finely toothed leaf with a whitish underside. Native to the southeastern US.
Narrow leaf, often on twisted branches in the corkscrew form. Chinese.
Long narrow finely toothed leaf, green on both sides. Ontario's largest native willow.
Three leaf shapes on one tree: oval, mitten-shaped and three-lobed; spicy smell when crushed. Carolinian zone.
Opposite compound leaf with 3 finely toothed leaflets; papery inflated seed pods.
Oval toothed leaf; camellia-like white flowers and patchy bark. Japanese ornamental.
Small glossy oval leaf; hanging white bell-shaped flowers. East Asian ornamental.
Large round leaf with a short tip; long chains of fragrant white flowers. East Asian ornamental.
Opposite oval smooth-edged leaf; creamy white flower plumes in early summer. Common street tree.
Soft flat needles arranged in two rows, shed in fall. Native to southeastern US swamps.
Large heart-shaped leaf with an uneven base and coarse teeth.
Small heart-shaped leaf with tufts of rusty hairs in the vein angles underneath. European street tree.
Heart-shaped leaf, between littleleaf linden and basswood in size. European hybrid.
Heart-shaped leaf with a white felt-like underside. Southeastern Europe.
Long compound leaf with 10-22 leaflets; young leaves eaten as a vegetable in China.
Short flat needles with two white stripes underneath on tiny stalks; small cones. Threatened by hemlock woolly adelgid.
Oval double-toothed leaf with an uneven base. Largely killed by Dutch elm disease.
Large rough double-toothed leaf, sometimes with 3 points at the tip. European.
Small glossy leathery leaf with single teeth; patchy flaking bark. East Asian.
Small rough round double-toothed leaf with an uneven base. European.
Small leaf with a nearly even base (unlike native elms) and single teeth. Asian; spreads readily in disturbed areas.
Large very rough leaf with double teeth; slimy inner bark.
Elm-like leaf with sharp single teeth curving toward the tip. East Asian street tree.
